---
title: "From linguistic records to probabilities"
---

A statistical analysis begins with a representation of the observations, not with the fitting of a model. An audio file might yield a table with one row per speaker, word, or vowel token, while a corpus might yield a table of documents, sentences, tokens, or lexical types. Each representation preserves some distinctions and removes others, and a later model can describe only the distinctions that remain in the dataset.

This module develops that point in two stages. The first stage concerns linguistic records and numerical patterns. The second builds a probability model one object at a time.

## From records to comparisons

We begin with [turning linguistic records into data](linguistic-data.qmd). That page separates a stored record from the unit represented by one row. It also asks which identifiers repeat and which variation disappears during aggregation.

The next page turns [a research question into a comparison](making-sense-of-data.qmd). It specifies the response, the linguistic predictor, the observations being compared, and the estimand. These decisions state what a later numerical result is supposed to mean.

[Zipf's law](zipfs-law.qmd) supplies the first worked linguistic pattern. The rank and frequency calculation is simple enough to do by hand, but its interpretation is not. The example separates describing a curve from explaining why that curve appears.

## From possibilities to a probability model

The probability sequence has a strict order. A [sample space](possibilities-and-events.qmd) specifies the possible outcomes, [events](events.qmd) group those outcomes, and a [sigma-algebra](event-spaces.qmd) specifies which groups are measurable. We then construct [generated sigma-algebras](generating-event-spaces.qmd) and assign probability with a [probability measure](probability-measures.qmd).

The remaining pages study relations among measurable events. [Mutual exclusivity](probability-concepts.qmd) concerns events that cannot occur together; [joint probability](joint-probability-of-events.qmd) assigns probability to an intersection; and [conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd) rescales probability within an event. [The product rule](probability-factorization.qmd), [Bayes' rule](bayes-rule.qmd), and [independence](independence.qmd) follow from these objects. Each page therefore depends only on objects introduced earlier in the sequence.

## The representational question

For any linguistic dataset, keep asking the same question:

> Which represented outcomes and distinctions make this probability statement meaningful?

If the answer is unavailable, the numerical calculation may be correct even though its linguistic interpretation is unsupported. The foundations sequence makes the representation explicit before introducing more elaborate models.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) places this chapter within the full course. Begin with [turning linguistic records into data](linguistic-data.qmd).
